serious_errors.materiality: A blanket Section 50 noncompliance attribution could wrongly discount separate correspondence and school-record corroboration. The excerpts establish criticism of certain witnesses, but do not fully resolve judicial treatment of each document.

important_omissions: The report does not set out the opposing provenance accounts: the plaintiff claimed Ram Piari acquired property using his money, while Raj Kumari said she bought it with her own money for Ram Piari. This matters to the High Court’s stranger-given-property limitation.

The report omits that the defendants claimed Ram Piari bequeathed the property by will to Parvin Kumari. It reports the trial court’s rejection of testamentary power without identifying the will beneficiary or distinguishing that finding from unresolved later validity.

Although it notes the two excluded cars, the report omits Raj Kumari’s distinct claim that they were hers with Ram Piari only a benamidar and the trial court’s finding that they belonged to Raj Kumari.

The report does not explain the defendants’ additional contention that the alleged custom did not apply to personal and self-acquired property, distinct from the High Court’s finding concerning property given by Raj Kumari.

The report omits the corroborating conduct of Paras Ram addressing the plaintiff as jija and fails to give the correct direction of the school-record sala designation, both relevant to marriage proof.

The report does not separately frame unresolved appellate/legal questions about the sufficiency and treatment of the marriage evidence, the limits of customary preference across property categories, and the effect of the will if the trial findings do not stand; the withheld target disposition cannot be supplied.
main_answer_reason: The report substantively reconstructs the claim, opposite trial and High Court findings, cohabitation presumption, disputed marriage witnesses, Section 50 standard, and the High Court’s custom/provenance/Hindu-law reasoning. It does not improperly assert a withheld final appellate result. However, it materially mistakes counsel for the appellant and reverses a familial relation in the school records; it also extends the High Court’s stated Section 50 objection beyond the identified witness evidence, with uncertain severity. Competing funding/title claims, the daughter’s will bequest, property-specific issues, and unresolved legal consequences receive insufficient treatment. These defects leave a meaningful but incomplete and partly inaccurate substantive answer rather than no answer or a wholly unsupported one.
uncertainties: The ultimate appellate reasoning and disposition are withheld; the High Court and trial findings are historical attributed findings only.

The excerpts do not establish that the High Court declared every correspondence or school exhibit inadmissible or noncompliant under Section 50; the quoted criticism specifically addresses certain witnesses.

The appellate narrative reports maternal testimony, a statement in the will and elopement witnesses, but the excerpts do not isolate which of these individual items the High Court itself expressly adopted as grounds rather than which were recounted in the later appellate discussion.

The true provenance and legal treatment of each property category, along with the will’s ultimate effect, cannot be established merely from the conflicting party accounts and prior findings in this allowed record.
